## computer-use
You have a computer-use MCP available (tools named `mcp__computer-use__*`). It lets you take screenshots of the user's desktop and control it with mouse clicks, keyboard input, and scrolling.

**Pick the right tool for the app.** Each tier trades speed/precision against coverage:

1. **Dedicated MCP for the app** — if the task is in an app that has its own MCP (Slack, Gmail, Calendar, Linear, etc.) and that MCP is connected, use it. API-backed tools are fast and precise.
2. **Chrome MCP** (`mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`) — if the target is a web app and there's no dedicated MCP for it, use the browser tools. DOM-aware, much faster than clicking pixels. If the Chrome extension isn't connected, ask the user to install it rather than falling through to computer use.
3. **Computer use** — for native desktop apps (Maps, Notes, Finder, Photos, System Settings, any third-party native app) and cross-app workflows. Computer use IS the right tool here — don't decline a native-app task just because there's no dedicated MCP for it.

This is about what's available, not error handling — if a dedicated MCP tool errors, debug or report it rather than silently retrying via a slower tier.

**Look before you assert.** If the user asks about app state (what's open, what's connected, what an app can do), take a screenshot and check before answering. Don't answer from memory — the user's setup or app version may differ from what you expect. If you're about to say an app doesn't support an action, that claim should be grounded in what you just saw on screen, not general knowledge. Similarly, `list_granted_applications` or a fresh `screenshot` is cheaper than a wrong assertion about what's running.

**Loading via ToolSearch — load in bulk, not one-by-one:** if computer-use tools are in the deferred list, load them ALL in a single ToolSearch call: `{ query: "computer-use", max_results: 30 }`. The keyword search matches the server-name substring in every tool name, so one query returns the entire toolkit. Don't use `select:` for individual tools — that's one round-trip per tool.

**Access flow:** before any computer-use action you must call `request_access` with the list of applications you need. The user approves each application explicitly, and you may need to call it again mid-task if you discover you need another application.

**Tiered apps:** some apps are granted at a restricted tier based on their category — the tier is displayed in the approval dialog and returned in the `request_access` response:
- **Browsers** (Safari, Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Arc, etc.) → tier **"read"**: visible in screenshots, but clicks and typing are blocked. You can read what's already on screen. For navigation, clicking, or form-filling, use the claude-in-chrome MCP (tools named `mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`; load via ToolSearch if deferred).
- **Terminals and IDEs** (Terminal, iTerm, VS Code, JetBrains, etc.) → tier **"click"**: visible and left-clickable, but typing, key presses, right-click, modifier-clicks, and drag-drop are blocked. You can click a Run button or scroll test output, but cannot type into the editor or integrated terminal, cannot right-click (the context menu has Paste), and cannot drag text onto them. For shell commands, use the Bash tool.
- **Everything else** → tier **"full"**: no restrictions.

The tier is enforced by the frontmost-app check: if a tier-"read" app is in front, `left_click` returns an error; if a tier-"click" app is in front, `type` and `right_click` return errors. The error tells you what tier the app has and what to do instead. `open_application` works at any tier — bringing an app forward is a read-level operation.

**Link safety — treat links in emails and messages as suspicious by default.**
- **Never click web links with computer-use tools.** If you encounter a link in a native app (Mail, Messages, a PDF, etc.), do NOT `left_click` it. Open the URL via the claude-in-chrome MCP instead.
- **See the full URL before following any link.** Visible link text can be misleading — hover or inspect to get the real destination.
- **Links from emails, messages, or unknown-sender documents are suspicious by default.** If the destination URL is at all unfamiliar or looks off, ask the user for confirmation before proceeding.
- **Inside the Chrome extension** you can click links with the extension's tools, but the suspicion check still applies — verify unfamiliar URLs with the user.

**Financial actions - do not execute trades or move money.** Budgeting and accounting apps (Quicken, YNAB, QuickBooks, etc.) are granted at full tier so you can categorize transactions, generate reports, and help the user organize their finances. But never execute a trade, place an order, send money, or initiate a transfer on the user's behalf - always ask the user to perform those actions themselves.

=================== ISSUE #2067 ===================
Cross-org clobber on connector install: same custom (key, version) last-writer-wins on one global connector_versions row [CLOSED/COMPLETED] by buremba
LABELS: 
BODY:
## Summary

Pre-existing vulnerability (predates #2045, discovered during its review): `connector_versions` was keyed only `(connector_key, version)` with `ON CONFLICT ... DO UPDATE`. Two organizations installing **different code** under the same custom key+version silently last-writer-win on one global row:

- Org B's install **overwrites the code org A executes** (feed sync, pushdown, webhooks, worker runs all resolve from the shared row).
- Any org could **read** (`get_connector_source`) and **activate** (`rollback_connector_version`) another org's uploaded artifact.

Prod impact scan (2026-07-21): 115 rows, 80 custom, 16 keys shared by >1 org, 7 live (key, version) cross-org collisions — all stock bundled names at bundled versions (harmless dedup, not deliberate forks), so no known malicious exploitation. The write path was exploitable by any org that could guess/observe another org's connector key+version.

## Fix

Shipped as the #2045 follow-up stack:
- #2064 — `organization_id` on `connector_versions` (partial unique arbiters) + dual-write
- #2065 — org-preferring resolution on every read + cross-org read/activate fence
- #2066 — backfill custom rows to owning orgs + retire shared custom writes

After #2066, org-supplied content exists only on the owning org's rows; the shared namespace holds bundled catalog pointers alone.

## Remaining

- [ ] After #2066 deploys: prune any shared custom rows recreated by old replicas during the rolling window (re-run the migration's DELETE statement).
- [ ] Verify prod post-deploy: `SELECT connector_key, version FROM connector_versions WHERE organization_id IS NULL AND (source_code IS NOT NULL OR compiled_code IS NOT NULL)` should return only orphans (no definition anywhere).
--- COMMENT by buremba ---
Resolved. The #2066 backfill migration was aborting in prod, which blocked the entire #2045 isolation rollout from deploying — so the two remaining items below could never run. Root cause + fix shipped in **#2071** (`af29895d`).

## What was wrong

The backfill `INSERT ... SELECT` joins `connector_definitions` and inserts `d.organization_id`. Bundled catalog definitions carry `organization_id IS NULL`; for those the INSERT re-emitted a *shared* (`organization_id IS NULL`) row that collided with the existing source row on the `connector_versions_shared_key_version` arbiter — which the INSERT's org-only `ON CONFLICT ... WHERE organization_id IS NOT NULL` clause does not cover — raising:

```
duplicate key value violates unique constraint "connector_versions_shared_key_version"
detail: Key (connector_key, version)=(capterra, 1.0.0) already exists.
```

21 bundled definitions in prod matched custom-bearing keys, so `summaries-app-lobu-migrate` failed (`BackoffLimitExceeded`) and Helm rolled back every attempt.

## Fix (#2071)

Gate the backfill INSERT on `AND d.organization_id IS NOT NULL` — bundled definitions own nothing, so only real org installs are backfill targets. Added a regression test seeding the exact prod shape (a NULL-org definition alongside a shared custom row); it reproduces the 23505 without the fix and passes with it.

## Deploy + verification (prod `owletto`, post-deploy)

- HelmRelease `summaries-app`: `Ready=True (UpgradeSucceeded)` — deploy unblocked, migrate job green.
- Migration `20260721130000` recorded in `schema_migrations`.
- `connector_versions`: 116 rows / 116 shared / 0 org-scoped → **163 / 34 shared / 129 org-scoped**. Org-supplied content now lives only on owning-org rows.

- [x] **Prune shared custom rows recreated by old replicas** — prune-check returns **0**; nothing to prune.
- [x] **Orphan-check returns only orphans** — returns one row, `microsoft.outlook 1.0.0` with zero `connector_definitions` for the key (a true orphan / sole copy, correctly left shared).

The shared namespace now holds bundled catalog pointers plus one legitimate orphan; no cross-org read/activate surface remains.

=================== ISSUE #2073 ===================
Flaky test: handleWebhookIngest rate limiting > 429 once the authenticated per-connection budget is exhausted [OPEN] by buremba
LABELS: 
BODY:
## Summary

`handleWebhookIngest rate limiting > 429 once the authenticated per-connection budget is exhausted` in `packages/server/src/gateway/__tests__/webhook-ingest.test.ts` is flaky in the `integration` CI job (gateway `bun:test` suite). It failed once on #2071's first CI run, then passed on a `--failed` rerun with no code change touching it (that PR only edited a connector migration + its test).

## Evidence

- Failing run: https://github.com/lobu-ai/lobu/actions/runs/29826237454/job/88620186155 — `1561 pass / 1 fail`, sole failure:
  ```
  error: expect(received).toBeDefined()
  (fail) handleWebhookIngest rate limiting > 429 once the authenticated per-connection budget is exhausted [137.32ms]
  ```
- Rerun of the same job: green. `main` at the parent commit (`bc7b22da`) is green on `integration`.
- Duration on the failing attempt was 137ms vs ~50ms on the sibling passing tests in the same suite — consistent with CI-load-induced timing.

## Likely cause

The test fires `WEBHOOK_INGEST_RATE_LIMIT.limit + 1` requests and asserts one returns 429:

```ts
for (let i = 0; i <= WEBHOOK_INGEST_RATE_LIMIT.limit; i++) {
  const res = await ingest(storedRow(), delivery({ i }, { headers: bearer }));
  if (res.status === 429) { limited = res; break; }
}
expect(limited).toBeDefined();
```

If the limiter uses a wall-clock window, a slow CI runner can let the window roll over mid-loop, so the per-connection budget refills before it's ever exhausted and no request hits 429 → `limited` stays `undefined`. `webhook-ingest.test.ts:633`.

## Suggested fix

Make the test independent of wall-clock timing — e.g. inject/fake the clock so all `limit+1` requests fall in one window, or drive the limiter's window deterministically rather than relying on real-time back-to-back `await`s. (Not urgent; it reruns green. Filing so a recurrence isn't mistaken for a real regression.)

=================== ISSUE #2100 ===================
Canvas entities land in $member because no 'canvas' entity type is ever provisioned [CLOSED/COMPLETED] by buremba
LABELS: 
BODY:
## What happens

`ensureCanvasEntity` needs an `entity_type_id` (the column is NOT NULL). It looks for a type with slug `canvas`, and when there isn't one it falls back to:

```sql
SELECT et.id FROM entity_types et
WHERE et.organization_id = $org AND et.deleted_at IS NULL AND et.backing_sql IS NULL
ORDER BY et.id ASC
LIMIT 1
```

`packages/server/src/utils/canvas-events.ts:124-136`

Nothing in the repo ever creates a `canvas` entity type — no migration, no default provisioning (the `'canvas'` in `default-provisioning.ts:481` is a `notification_channel` value, not a type). So the fallback is not an edge case, it's the **only** path, in every org.

Lowest-id non-view type is almost always `$member`, since it's provisioned first.

## Prod evidence (buremba)

```
entity_types:  canvas_exists = false;  lowest id = 16 ($member)

entities WHERE entity_type = '$member':
  canvas_pollution  16
  real_member        2
```

And it's user-visible — `entities.list({ entity_type: "$member" })` returns:

```
Canvas · watcher 34, Canvas · watcher 33, ... (15 of these)
Burak                                        <- the only real member, buried at #15
```

## Why it matters beyond cosmetics

`$member` is a privileged, access-controlled type: `canSeeMemberList` gates it and member emails get hidden (`manage_entity.ts:751`, `:854`). Canvas objects inheriting that type means system-internal rows are being carried through member-scoped access policy and shown in the member roster.

The docstring at `canvas-events.ts:71-73` says it falls back to "a sensible default" — the actual behavior (arbitrary lowest-id type) isn't that.

## Suggested direction

Provision a real `canvas` entity type (system-owned, like `$member`/`$resource` — the `$` prefix convention already exists for exactly this), and have `ensureCanvasEntity` create-or-get it instead of borrowing an unrelated type. Failing to anchor is better than anchoring to `$member`.

Existing rows need a backfill to move the 16 mislabeled entities off `$member`.

Found during a prod e2e verification sweep.
=================== ISSUE #2146 ===================
Close governed metric correctness gaps and wire `reflectMetrics()` end to end [OPEN] by buremba
LABELS: 
BODY:
## Summary

Lobu already has a working entity-bound metric path:

`defineEntityType()` → `lobu apply` → `entity_types.metrics_config` → `list_metrics` → `query_metric`.

This issue is **not** a metric-layer rewrite. It tracks the confirmed gaps between the public metric contracts and their current runtime behaviour, plus the incomplete warehouse/native-semantic-layer federation path.

## Confirmed gaps

### 1. `reflectMetrics()` is exposed but never executed

The connector SDK exposes and forwards `reflectMetrics(ctx)`:

- `packages/connector-sdk/src/connector-types.ts`
- `packages/connector-sdk/src/connector-runtime.ts`
- `packages/connector-sdk/src/define-connector.ts`

However, the connector executor protocol has no `reflect` job/result mode, and `child-runner.ts` never calls `instance.reflectMetrics()`:

- `packages/connector-worker/src/executor/interface.ts`
- `packages/connector-worker/src/executor/child-runner.ts`

As a result, a connector can implement `reflectMetrics()`, but the platform does not invoke it, persist its contributions, refresh them, remove stale contributions, or expose them through the governed metric tools.

### 2. Reflected metric contributions cannot run through `query_metric`

`EntityTypeContribution` describes an externally governed relation using:

- `backing.sql`
- `backing.connection`
- reflected measures with `grain`, governance and `safeDimensions`

These measures intentionally do not contain event-backed `agg`, `expr` or `eventSet` fields.

Current consumers assume event-backed metrics only:

- `list_metrics` reads `metrics_config` and expects each measure to have `agg` and `eventSet`.
- `runMetric()` loads only `entity_types.id` and `metrics_config`.
- `runMetric()` always calls the event-stream compiler.
- It never loads `backing_sql` / `backing_source` or routes through connector query pushdown.

Relevant files:

- `packages/connector-sdk/src/metrics.ts`
- `packages/server/src/tools/admin/list_metrics.ts`
- `packages/server/src/metrics/run-metric.ts`
- `packages/server/src/metrics/compiler.ts`
- `packages/server/src/tools/admin/query_sql.ts`

### 3. `safeDimensions` is declared but not enforced

`Measure.safeDimensions` and `ReflectedMeasure.safeDimensions` are intended to prevent invalid fan-out/grouping combinations.

The current compiler accepts any requested dimension that exists in `metrics.dimensions`; it never checks the measure's `safeDimensions`.

This can return semantically invalid or double-counted results while appearing governed.

Relevant file:

- `packages/server/src/metrics/compiler.ts`

### 4. Segment grain and placement are ignored

The SDK declares:

```ts
on: 'event' | 'entity'
appliedBefore?: 'dedupe' | 'aggregate'
```

The compiler currently places every segment predicate inside the initial event query before entity resolution and deduplication. It does not inspect either property.

Consequences:

- `on: 'entity'` is not honoured.
- `appliedBefore: 'aggregate'` behaves as pre-dedupe filtering.
- Persisted configuration can claim semantics the runtime does not implement.

Relevant files:

- `packages/connector-sdk/src/metrics.ts`
- `packages/server/src/metrics/compiler.ts`

### 5. Apply accepts metric configurations that only fail at query time

The public contract currently accepts:

- `EventSet.by: 'alias' | 'window' | 'link'`
- `reads: 'current' | 'raw' | { asOf }`
- `factIdentity`

The compiler currently supports only:

- `by: 'alias'`
- `reads: 'current'`

The validator checks references and basic shape, but does not reject unsupported resolver/read modes or validate all semantic references such as `safeDimensions`.

This permits a successful deployment followed by a runtime `NotImplemented` failure when an agent queries the metric.

Relevant files:

- `packages/connector-sdk/src/metrics.ts`
- `packages/server/src/metrics/compiler.ts`
- `packages/server/src/tools/admin/manage_entity_schema.ts`
- `packages/cli/src/commands/_lib/apply/define-config.ts`

### 6. `dedupeKey` does not strictly identify one fact

The compiler uses `SELECT DISTINCT`, but the distinct row includes:

- entity ID
- requested dimension values
- measure value
- declared dedupe-key values

If two rows share the declared dedupe key but disagree on the measure value, both survive. The current behaviour is therefore closer to "dedupe identical metric rows" than "these fields identify one fact."

The metric contract needs an explicit representative/conflict policy, implemented with `DISTINCT ON`, a window function, or equivalent deterministic selection.

Relevant file:

- `packages/server/src/metrics/compiler.ts`

### 7. Metric resolution depends on a duplicated alias projection

Event-backed entity metrics resolve against `entities.metadata.aliases`, while canonical identity resolution uses `entity_identities` and durable event attribution.

The ingestion path has to keep both representations synchronized; the code explicitly notes that missing aliases cause metrics to silently drop events.

Relevant files:

- `packages/server/src/utils/entity-link-upsert.ts`
- `packages/server/src/metrics/compiler.ts`

This is not necessarily a blocker for v1, but `by: 'link'` should eventually use durable attribution/identity links and become the preferred resolver where available.

### Phase 1 — correctness and fail-fast validation

- [ ] Enforce `safeDimensions` in `compileMetricSql()`.
- [ ] Validate that every `safeDimensions` entry names a declared dimension.
- [ ] Implement segment `on` / `appliedBefore` semantics, or reject unsupported combinations during apply.
- [ ] Reject `window`, `link`, non-current reads and `factIdentity` during apply until they are executable.
- [ ] Define deterministic `dedupeKey` conflict/representative semantics.

- [ ] Persist contributions with at least connector key/version, connection slug, freshness and contribution identity.
- [ ] Define collision/override rules between locally authored and reflected entity types/measures.
- [ ] Remove or mark stale contributions when reflection no longer returns them.
- [ ] Normalize event-backed and reflected metrics in `list_metrics` while retaining producer/source metadata.
- [ ] Make `runMetric()` branch by producer:
  - event-backed → current compiler path
  - reflected → live connector query pushdown using `backing.sql` and `backing.connection`
- [ ] Return source, freshness, grain and warnings from `query_metric`.

=================== ISSUE #2148 ===================
Slack Grid: one workspace can hold two active connections (E… vs T… tenant keys) [OPEN] by buremba
LABELS: 
BODY:
## Problem

A Slack Grid workspace can be recorded under **either** identifier:
- the enterprise id (`E…`) — an org-wide install (`is_enterprise_install=true`)
- the workspace id (`T…`) — a per-workspace install

`connections_active_chat_tenant` is unique on `(organization_id, connector_key, external_tenant_id)`. Two different strings ⇒ two distinct tenants ⇒ both rows stay active for one workspace.

**Observed in prod 2026-07-23:** connections 430 (`E0BDSKL1KJL`) and 448 (`T0BCYB6JV3L`) were both active for LobuSandbox for ~3m21s. It was resolved by an explicit `deleteConnection`, not by any reconciler — nothing heals this automatically.

## Actual harm (re-rated down)

Routing today is **deterministic**, not ambiguous — `slack-connection-coordinator` precedence is exact-team → org-wide → sole-active. Two active rows do **not** cause misrouting.

The real harm is narrower: **binding/grant fragmentation across two connection ids** — channel Behaviors, `/lobu link` bindings, and Builder admin grants attach to whichever id was current, so they silently split across the pair.

## Why the obvious fix is wrong

Attempted in #2143 (closed). Widening the projection demote to retire the other-keyed row causes **dropped Slack messages**:

- routing selects installs from `app_installations`, which a projection demote never touches
- `ensureConnectionRunning` (chat-instance-manager.ts:1798-1806) returns false on a stopped projection and tears down any running instance
- `paused` → `stopped` via `connectionsStatusToLegacy`; `getConnection` reads only the projection, no install fallback
- nothing revives it (`sweepConnectionHealth` skips `stopped`; boot warm-start removed) ⇒ **indefinite 503**

Also surfaced there: a cross-key row-lock deadlock (T…-keyed advisories held while row-updating the E…-keyed row, and vice versa) on a transaction with no `withChatConnectionDeadlockRetry` (slack-installations.ts:364).

And demoting the org-wide install may be semantically wrong: an `E…` install legitimately serves every sibling workspace, so retiring it because one workspace reinstalled strands the other N-1.

## Open design questions

1. **Is coexistence actually correct?** Routing precedence already disambiguates. Maybe `E…`/`T…` should coexist and there should be no demote at all — in which case only the binding/grant fragmentation needs fixing.
2. **If reconciliation is wanted**, it requires: two-table atomicity (`connections` + `app_installations`), an enterprise-scoped advisory taken before any row lock in both writers, and a backfill for pre-existing rows.
3. **Cheaper alternative worth evaluating first:** connection-id canonicalization at binding time — resolve bindings/grants through a stable workspace identity rather than the raw connection id. Addresses the actual harm without a tenant-key migration.

## Cleanup

`slack-installations.ts:337` claims a "read-fallback to `getSlackInstallById`" that does not exist for this path (its only external consumer is `authz/slack-acl-sync.ts:297`). The stale comment misled a review round into believing a safety net existed.

## Notes

- `config->'chatMetadata'->>'enterpriseId'` is empty on every existing prod connections row; the same data **is** populated on `app_installations.metadata` (`enterprise_id`, `is_enterprise_install`), so any detector or backfill should read from there.
- Interim option: a read-side detector that logs when one org holds two live chat connections sharing an `enterprise_id`. Visibility, no write-path risk.
--- COMMENT by buremba ---
## Decision: preferred long-term direction

**Make bindings resolve by workspace identity, not by connection id.**

Today channel Behaviors, `/lobu link`, and the Builder admin grant attach to a specific `connections` row — a bookkeeping record that changes on reinstall. That is the actual defect: the binding is anchored to something transient when the intent is "this Slack workspace."

Fix that and the duplicate becomes harmless: `E…`/`T…` rows coexist, routing precedence (exact-team → org-wide → sole-active) already delivers messages deterministically, and bindings survive a reinstall.

Rejected: forcing one active row per workspace. Attempted in #2143 — causes indefinite 503s (dropped Slack messages), needs two-table atomicity plus a new enterprise-scoped lock protocol, and is arguably semantically wrong (an org-wide `E…` install legitimately serves every sibling workspace; retiring it strands the other N-1).

Scope signal: 5 live `behavior_message_subscriptions` rows on Slack today, so the migration surface is currently tiny. Worth doing properly before that grows.

## Backfill: not needed

Checked prod — one active Slack install (LobuSandbox, `T0BCYB6JV3L`), and it already has its `chat_user_identities` link (written on tonight's reinstall via #2136). **Zero rows to backfill.**

Replace the backfill idea with a **self-heal guard**: when an active install has no identity link for its installer, create it (or log loudly). Covers future installs that predate a claim without a migration against an empty set.

## Interim

Read-side detector: log when one org holds two live chat connections sharing an `enterprise_id` (read from `app_installations.metadata->>'enterprise_id'`, which is populated — the projection's `chatMetadata.enterpriseId` is not). Visibility only, no write-path risk.

Shipped as the #2045 follow-up stack:
- #2064 — `organization_id` on `connector_versions` (partial unique arbiters) + dual-write
- #2065 — org-preferring resolution on every read + cross-org read/activate fence
- #2066 — backfill custom rows to owning orgs + retire shared custom writes

After #2066, org-supplied content exists only on the owning org's rows; the shared namespace holds bundled catalog pointers alone.

- [ ] After #2066 deploys: prune any shared custom rows recreated by old replicas during the rolling window (re-run the migration's DELETE statement).

--- COMMENT by buremba ---
Resolved. The #2066 backfill migration was aborting in prod, which blocked the entire #2045 isolation rollout from deploying — so the two remaining items below could never run. Root cause + fix shipped in **#2071** (`af29895d`).

## What was wrong

The backfill `INSERT ... SELECT` joins `connector_definitions` and inserts `d.organization_id`. Bundled catalog definitions carry `organization_id IS NULL`; for those the INSERT re-emitted a *shared* (`organization_id IS NULL`) row that collided with the existing source row on the `connector_versions_shared_key_version` arbiter — which the INSERT's org-only `ON CONFLICT ... WHERE organization_id IS NOT NULL` clause does not cover — raising:

```
duplicate key value violates unique constraint "connector_versions_shared_key_version"
detail: Key (connector_key, version)=(capterra, 1.0.0) already exists.
```

21 bundled definitions in prod matched custom-bearing keys, so `summaries-app-lobu-migrate` failed (`BackoffLimitExceeded`) and Helm rolled back every attempt.

## Fix (#2071)

Gate the backfill INSERT on `AND d.organization_id IS NOT NULL` — bundled definitions own nothing, so only real org installs are backfill targets. Added a regression test seeding the exact prod shape (a NULL-org definition alongside a shared custom row); it reproduces the 23505 without the fix and passes with it.

Flaky test: handleWebhookIngest rate limiting > 429 once the authenticated per-connection budget is exhausted [OPEN] by buremba
LABELS: 
BODY:
## Summary

`handleWebhookIngest rate limiting > 429 once the authenticated per-connection budget is exhausted` in `packages/server/src/gateway/__tests__/webhook-ingest.test.ts` is flaky in the `integration` CI job (gateway `bun:test` suite). It failed once on #2071's first CI run, then passed on a `--failed` rerun with no code change touching it (that PR only edited a connector migration + its test).

## Evidence

- Failing run: https://github.com/lobu-ai/lobu/actions/runs/29826237454/job/88620186155 — `1561 pass / 1 fail`, sole failure:
  ```
  error: expect(received).toBeDefined()
  (fail) handleWebhookIngest rate limiting > 429 once the authenticated per-connection budget is exhausted [137.32ms]
  ```
- Rerun of the same job: green. `main` at the parent commit (`bc7b22da`) is green on `integration`.
- Duration on the failing attempt was 137ms vs ~50ms on the sibling passing tests in the same suite — consistent with CI-load-induced timing.

## Likely cause

The test fires `WEBHOOK_INGEST_RATE_LIMIT.limit + 1` requests and asserts one returns 429:

```ts
for (let i = 0; i <= WEBHOOK_INGEST_RATE_LIMIT.limit; i++) {
  const res = await ingest(storedRow(), delivery({ i }, { headers: bearer }));
  if (res.status === 429) { limited = res; break; }
}
expect(limited).toBeDefined();
```

If the limiter uses a wall-clock window, a slow CI runner can let the window roll over mid-loop, so the per-connection budget refills before it's ever exhausted and no request hits 429 → `limited` stays `undefined`. `webhook-ingest.test.ts:633`.

## Suggested fix

Make the test independent of wall-clock timing — e.g. inject/fake the clock so all `limit+1` requests fall in one window, or drive the limiter's window deterministically rather than relying on real-time back-to-back `await`s. (Not urgent; it reruns green. Filing so a recurrence isn't mistaken for a real regression.)

=================== ISSUE #2100 ===================
Canvas entities land in $member because no 'canvas' entity type is ever provisioned [CLOSED/COMPLETED] by buremba
LABELS: 
BODY:
## What happens

`ensureCanvasEntity` needs an `entity_type_id` (the column is NOT NULL). It looks for a type with slug `canvas`, and when there isn't one it falls back to:

```sql
SELECT et.id FROM entity_types et
WHERE et.organization_id = $org AND et.deleted_at IS NULL AND et.backing_sql IS NULL
ORDER BY et.id ASC
LIMIT 1
```

`packages/server/src/utils/canvas-events.ts:124-136`

Nothing in the repo ever creates a `canvas` entity type — no migration, no default provisioning (the `'canvas'` in `default-provisioning.ts:481` is a `notification_channel` value, not a type). So the fallback is not an edge case, it's the **only** path, in every org.

Lowest-id non-view type is almost always `$member`, since it's provisioned first.

## Prod evidence (buremba)

```
entity_types:  canvas_exists = false;  lowest id = 16 ($member)

entities WHERE entity_type = '$member':
  canvas_pollution  16
  real_member        2
```

And it's user-visible — `entities.list({ entity_type: "$member" })` returns:

```
Canvas · watcher 34, Canvas · watcher 33, ... (15 of these)
Burak                                        <- the only real member, buried at #15
```

## Why it matters beyond cosmetics

`$member` is a privileged, access-controlled type: `canSeeMemberList` gates it and member emails get hidden (`manage_entity.ts:751`, `:854`). Canvas objects inheriting that type means system-internal rows are being carried through member-scoped access policy and shown in the member roster.

The docstring at `canvas-events.ts:71-73` says it falls back to "a sensible default" — the actual behavior (arbitrary lowest-id type) isn't that.

## Suggested direction

Provision a real `canvas` entity type (system-owned, like `$member`/`$resource` — the `$` prefix convention already exists for exactly this), and have `ensureCanvasEntity` create-or-get it instead of borrowing an unrelated type. Failing to anchor is better than anchoring to `$member`.

Existing rows need a backfill to move the 16 mislabeled entities off `$member`.

Found during a prod e2e verification sweep.

The real harm is narrower: **binding/grant fragmentation across two connection ids** — channel Behaviors, `/lobu link` bindings, and Builder admin grants attach to whichever id was current, so they silently split across the pair.

## Why the obvious fix is wrong

Attempted in #2143 (closed). Widening the projection demote to retire the other-keyed row causes **dropped Slack messages**:

- routing selects installs from `app_installations`, which a projection demote never touches
- `ensureConnectionRunning` (chat-instance-manager.ts:1798-1806) returns false on a stopped projection and tears down any running instance
- `paused` → `stopped` via `connectionsStatusToLegacy`; `getConnection` reads only the projection, no install fallback
- nothing revives it (`sweepConnectionHealth` skips `stopped`; boot warm-start removed) ⇒ **indefinite 503**

Also surfaced there: a cross-key row-lock deadlock (T…-keyed advisories held while row-updating the E…-keyed row, and vice versa) on a transaction with no `withChatConnectionDeadlockRetry` (slack-installations.ts:364).

And demoting the org-wide install may be semantically wrong: an `E…` install legitimately serves every sibling workspace, so retiring it because one workspace reinstalled strands the other N-1.

## Open design questions

1. **Is coexistence actually correct?** Routing precedence already disambiguates. Maybe `E…`/`T…` should coexist and there should be no demote at all — in which case only the binding/grant fragmentation needs fixing.
2. **If reconciliation is wanted**, it requires: two-table atomicity (`connections` + `app_installations`), an enterprise-scoped advisory taken before any row lock in both writers, and a backfill for pre-existing rows.
3. **Cheaper alternative worth evaluating first:** connection-id canonicalization at binding time — resolve bindings/grants through a stable workspace identity rather than the raw connection id. Addresses the actual harm without a tenant-key migration.

## Cleanup

`slack-installations.ts:337` claims a "read-fallback to `getSlackInstallById`" that does not exist for this path (its only external consumer is `authz/slack-acl-sync.ts:297`). The stale comment misled a review round into believing a safety net existed.

## Notes

- `config->'chatMetadata'->>'enterpriseId'` is empty on every existing prod connections row; the same data **is** populated on `app_installations.metadata` (`enterprise_id`, `is_enterprise_install`), so any detector or backfill should read from there.
- Interim option: a read-side detector that logs when one org holds two live chat connections sharing an `enterprise_id`. Visibility, no write-path risk.
--- COMMENT by buremba ---
## Decision: preferred long-term direction

**Make bindings resolve by workspace identity, not by connection id.**

Today channel Behaviors, `/lobu link`, and the Builder admin grant attach to a specific `connections` row — a bookkeeping record that changes on reinstall. That is the actual defect: the binding is anchored to something transient when the intent is "this Slack workspace."

Fix that and the duplicate becomes harmless: `E…`/`T…` rows coexist, routing precedence (exact-team → org-wide → sole-active) already delivers messages deterministically, and bindings survive a reinstall.

Rejected: forcing one active row per workspace. Attempted in #2143 — causes indefinite 503s (dropped Slack messages), needs two-table atomicity plus a new enterprise-scoped lock protocol, and is arguably semantically wrong (an org-wide `E…` install legitimately serves every sibling workspace; retiring it strands the other N-1).

Scope signal: 5 live `behavior_message_subscriptions` rows on Slack today, so the migration surface is currently tiny. Worth doing properly before that grows.

## Backfill: not needed

Checked prod — one active Slack install (LobuSandbox, `T0BCYB6JV3L`), and it already has its `chat_user_identities` link (written on tonight's reinstall via #2136). **Zero rows to backfill.**

Replace the backfill idea with a **self-heal guard**: when an active install has no identity link for its installer, create it (or log loudly). Covers future installs that predate a claim without a migration against an empty set.

## Interim

Read-side detector: log when one org holds two live chat connections sharing an `enterprise_id` (read from `app_installations.metadata->>'enterprise_id'`, which is populated — the projection's `chatMetadata.enterpriseId` is not). Visibility only, no write-path risk.

Let's say I have 10 users whom I want to isolate + give access to their gmail/calendar over telegram, how many telegram bots do I need to configure? 10 or just 1? 2. Assuming I only need 1 bot, what happenes if 2 of these users and the telegram bot all join in a group and tries to query an MCP server, does lobu still answer to user 1 using credentials 1 and user 2 using credentials 2? or something else? 3. Can these credentials be updated over telegram by the users themselves? Thanks! --- COMMENT by buremba --- 1. Just **1 bot**. Telegram identity is keyed per user, so in DMs each of your 10 users gets their own isolated agent and context (`telegram-{userId}`) — one bot token serves all of them with separate credentials. You don't need 10 bots. 2. In a **group**, though, the space is keyed by the chat rather than the sender (`telegram-g-{chatId}`), so a group is a single shared identity. It does **not** split user 1's credentials from user 2's inside the group — per-user isolation is a DM property, not a group one. If you need each user to query with their own credentials, that happens in their DM with the bot. 3. Yes — each user connects their own Gmail/Calendar through their own DM/auth flow, so credentials stay per-user and are managed by the users themselves. --- COMMENT by bilogic --- Great! The reason I asked about group chats was, if a user has trouble setting up their email, I want support be in a group chat to help resolve their problem instead of them sending tons of screenshots to support From the way you phrase it, it sounds possible to have a group credential, am I right? --- COMMENT by bilogic --- ``` lobu-app | [2026-07-24 07:19:04] [info] [chat-message-bridge] Processing inbound message lobu-app | [2026-07-24 07:19:04] [warn] [chat-message-bridge] No channel Behavior and connection has no owning agent — dropping message ``` Is there any step by step documentation on how to set things up? I'm facing big challenges every step of the way --- COMMENT by buremba --- Answering the group-credentials question, then the log you hit — which is a real bug, not a misconfiguration on your side. On group credentials: not in the sense you're hoping for. A group is a single shared identity (`telegram-g-{chatId}`), so there's no per-user credential split inside it — but that also means the group does not get access to any user's connected Gmail or Calendar. Those are attached to each user's own DM identity (`telegram-{userId}`) and stay there. So a support person in the group can see the conversation and help the user talk through the problem, but the bot in that group cannot act on the user's mailbox, and the user's credentials are never exposed to the group. For a support-triage flow that's usually what you want; if you need the agent to actually operate on the user's mailbox while support watches, that has to happen in the user's DM. On the dropped message: `No channel Behavior and connection has no owning agent` means the inbound message resolved to no agent — the connection has no owning agent and the channel has no Behavior bound to it, so there's nothing to route to. What makes this a bug is the silence. On Slack, the same dead end posts a "this channel isn't linked yet" notice back into the conversation with a link to fix it. On Telegram it just logs a warning server-side and drops, so from the chat side the bot appears to ignore you with no indication why. Same root cause, one surface tells you and the other doesn't. Sorry for sending you down two dead ends. On `lobu` not being available in Docker: correct, and it isn't an alias you're missing. The app image's runtime stage copies `packages/core`, `plugin-*`, `agent-worker`, `connector-*`, `server` and so on, but it never copies `packages/cli`, so no `lobu` binary is installed and the container starts the server bundle directly via `start.sh`. Quick fix: install Node 22+ and re-run: ``` nvm install 22 && nvm use 22 # or: brew install node@22 npx @lobu/cli@latest run ``` The 22 floor comes from the isolated-vm sandbox we run agent code in — it only ships native builds for Node 22–24 and 26+. I've just merged a fix (#2175) so that running on an unsupported Node fails with a clear "Lobu needs Node.js 22 or newer" message that explains the requirement, instead of the cryptic undici error. It'll be in the next release. If you upgrade Node in the meantime you should be unblocked right away — and once the new version is out, could you give it a try and confirm the message shows up as expected? --- COMMENT by bilogic --- Thanks for getting back, testing it right now, yes I managed to figure out it was a node issue before you replied. For background info, my docker compose actually ran, but alot of routes (URLs) are broken, basically I wasn't able to add a provider properly. I tried both localhost and reverse proxy, that's when I decided to try the CLI instead. --- COMMENT by bilogic --- Still can't get started - If I run as root postgres complains and terminates - If I run as a lobu user, `npm install` works but `... run` keeps terminating with no errors ``` root@sqlserver2025:/my-lobu# sudo -u lobu npx @lobu/cli@latest run Need to install the following packages: @lobu/cli@14.0.0 Ok to proceed? (y) y npm warn ERESOLVE overriding peer dependency npm warn While resolving: marked-terminal@7.3.0 npm warn Found: marked@17.0.6 npm warn node_modules/@lobu/cli/node_modules/marked npm warn marked@"^17.0.4" from @lobu/cli@14.0.0 npm warn node_modules/@lobu/cli npm warn @lobu/cli@"14.0.0" from the root project npm warn npm warn Could not resolve dependency: npm warn peer marked@">=1 <16" from marked-terminal@7.3.0 npm warn node_modules/@lobu/cli/node_modules/marked-terminal npm warn marked-terminal@"^7.3.0" from @lobu/cli@14.0.0 npm warn node_modules/@lobu/cli npm warn npm warn Conflicting peer dependency: marked@15.0.12 npm warn node_modules/marked npm warn peer marked@">=1 <16" from marked-terminal@7.3.0 npm warn node_modules/@lobu/cli/node_modules/marked-terminal npm warn marked-terminal@"^7.3.0" from @lobu/cli@14.0.0 npm warn node_modules/@lobu/cli npm warn deprecated prebuild-install@7.1.3: No longer maintained. I ran the CLI in a "local" docker container for isolation, thus localhost doesn't cut it. Switching back to tackling docker URL errors. --- COMMENT by bilogic --- I moved on to https://github.com/lobu-ai/lobu/issues/2183 where I managed to get it working =================== ISSUE #2183 =================== Docker 404 errors [CLOSED/COMPLETED] by bilogic LABELS: bug BODY: **Describe the bug** Many 404 errors when using a reverse proxy and docker **To Reproduce** Steps to reproduce the behavior: 1. Used the provided docker-compose.yaml 2. Reverse proxy to docker container port 3. Manage to create an account for login 4. But unable to do anything else, no models, no chats etc, all sorts of 404 errors 5. I was able to create an organization, but it linked to a prefixed URL.. https://lobu-example.com -> https://organization.lobu-example.com 6. Can we have it on a path instead of a subdomain? **Expected behavior** I should be able to at least to chat with it **Screenshots** N/A **Environment** - Runtime (local/systemd/managed host): docker - Platform (Slack/Telegram/Discord/etc.): unconfigured as it is docker - Lobu version: docker pull ghcr.io/lobu-ai/lobu-app:20260724-034552 **Additional context** No --- COMMENT by bilogic --- Ok, it finally worked after I further mapped my own subdomain, is there an option to put the organization on a path instead? --- COMMENT by buremba --- Glad you got it working, and sorry it took mapping a wildcard subdomain to get there. Answering your question directly, then the underlying bug. On paths vs subdomains: the API is already path-scoped. Everything under `/api/:orgSlug/...` takes the org as a path segment, so there's no architectural requirement for a subdomain. The subdomain layer is an optional convenience — a middleware reads `{org}.{zone}` off the Host header and sets the org from it, with the zone coming from `AUTH_COOKIE_DOMAIN` if set, otherwise the `PUBLIC_GATEWAY_URL` hostname. On a subdomain host it also 301s HTML GETs that carry a redundant `/{org}` prefix down to the stripped path. That last part is what bit you. The compose example ships `PUBLIC_GATEWAY_URL: http://localhost:8787/lobu` and sets no `AUTH_COOKIE_DOMAIN`. Behind a reverse proxy on your own domain, the browser origin no longer matches that configured origin, so the org link got built against the subdomain zone while the app was served from the apex — hence being able to register but then 404ing on models, chats, and everything else. So the real defect is that the documented self-host path doesn't tell you to set `PUBLIC_GATEWAY_URL` (and `AUTH_COOKIE_DOMAIN` if you want per-org hosts) to your actual external URL, and nothing validates the mismatch or fails loudly. Two things to fix, and I'm keeping this open for both: make `docker-compose.example.yml` plus the self-host docs cover the reverse-proxy case with the external URL called out, and add a startup check that warns when the served origin can't match the configured `PUBLIC_GATEWAY_URL` instead of degrading into scattered 404s. Worth confirming for your setup: with `PUBLIC_GATEWAY_URL` pointed at your apex domain and `AUTH_COOKIE_DOMAIN` left unset, the apex should work without the wildcard subdomain mapping. If it still redirects you to a subdomain after that, tell me and I'll treat the redirect itself as the bug rather than the config. --- COMMENT by buremba --- Thanks for the detail, the redirect to `organization.lobu-example.com` is the actual cause here rather than a separate quirk. Org scope is resolved from the Host header — `{org}.{zone}`, where the zone comes from `AUTH_COOKIE_DOMAIN` or falls back to the hostname in `PUBLIC_GATEWAY_URL`. So once you've created an org, the app sends you to a subdomain, and if your reverse proxy only forwards the apex you get a host with no resolvable org. Scope resolution then throws at the bare origin and the UI renders as 404s, which lines up with "no models, no chats, all sorts of 404 errors". Two things you can try right now, both without code changes: Point a wildcard at the container. If you can add `*.lobu-example.com` to DNS and your proxy, and set `PUBLIC_GATEWAY_URL=https://lobu-example.com` plus `AUTH_COOKIE_DOMAIN=.lobu-example.com`, the existing subdomain path should work as designed. This is the closest to how the hosted version runs, so it's the best-tested route. If wildcards aren't an option, note that path-based routing already partly exists — the frontend has an `/$owner/...` route, so `https://lobu-example.com/your-org/...` may get you further than the apex alone. I'd treat this as a workaround rather than a supported mode; there's no self-host flag today that makes it the default, and I haven't verified the whole app under it. On the actual ask — making path-based the supported setup for self-hosting — I think that's the right direction, since requiring wildcard DNS is a real barrier for anyone behind a single reverse proxy. I don't want to half-do it though: the pieces that need to agree are host-based scope extraction, the post-org-creation redirect, and auth cookie scoping (cookies on a shared path don't isolate orgs the way separate subdomains do, so that needs thought rather than a quick switch). Leaving this open as the tracking issue for that. Could you share what your proxy is (nginx/Caddy/Traefik) and whether wildcard DNS is available to you? That tells me whether the wildcard route unblocks you today, and it's useful input on how common the constraint is. --- COMMENT by bilogic --- Thanks, I'm using nginx proxy manager, likely moving to Caddy/Traefik. I do have wildcard certs in place today, but I would need a separate domain just for lobu, because today it is, https://service.my-domain.com, and I have many services on my homelab, it's going to be confusing to mix them up. =================== ISSUE #2184 =================== `latest` docker image should be tagged to release, not every push [CLOSED/COMPLETED] by bilogic LABELS: bug BODY: 1. The `latest` should tied to official releases, e.g. 14.2.0 instead of every other commit such as `20260724-034552` 2. It's quite impossible to figure out which is 14.2.0 --- COMMENT by buremba --- Both points are fair and this is a real packaging bug, not just a preference. You're right that `latest` currently moves on every push to `main`. The build workflow tags each image with a UTC timestamp and also pushes `latest` on the default branch, so `latest` tracks the tip of main rather than a release. For a self-hoster that means `docker pull ...:latest` gives you whatever merged most recently, which is not what the tag implies. On point 2, the reason you can't find a `14.2.0` image is that no such tag exists — the npm packages are versioned (14.2.0, 14.3.0) but the images are only ever tagged with the timestamp, so there's currently no way to map an image back to a release version at all. That's the more serious half of this report. One constraint worth flagging so the fix doesn't surprise you: our production deploy uses Flux, whose ImagePolicy matches the `^(\d{8})-(\d{6})$` timestamp pattern, and that policy lives in a separate repo. So the timestamp tags have to keep being published — the fix is to *add* semver tags (`14.3.0`, `14.3`, `14`) and repoint `latest` at the release build, not to change the existing scheme. That makes it an additive change to the release workflow. Marking this as a bug. Until it lands, pin the explicit timestamp tag you've tested rather than `latest`, since `latest` will keep moving under you. --- COMMENT by buremba --- Good catch, both parts were real. PR #2241 has the fix. `latest` was being pushed on every commit to main, which is why it kept landing on things like `20260724-034552`. It now only moves when a release is actually published, and the images get a semver tag at the same time, so `ghcr.io/lobu-ai/lobu-app:14.3.0` will work from the next release onward. Prereleases get their version tag but don't move `latest`. The timestamp tags aren't going away — our deploy automation selects images by that pattern, so they keep getting pushed on every main build. They just stop being what `latest` points at. One thing worth flagging: this takes effect from the next release, so `14.3.0` and earlier won't be retroactively tagged. Once it's out, pinning a version in your compose file is the safer setup anyway, and I've added a comment in `docker-compose.example.yml` showing that.

Answering your question directly, then the underlying bug. On paths vs subdomains: the API is already path-scoped. Everything under `/api/:orgSlug/...` takes the org as a path segment, so there's no architectural requirement for a subdomain. The subdomain layer is an optional convenience — a middleware reads `{org}.{zone}` off the Host header and sets the org from it, with the zone coming from `AUTH_COOKIE_DOMAIN` if set, otherwise the `PUBLIC_GATEWAY_URL` hostname. On a subdomain host it also 301s HTML GETs that carry a redundant `/{org}` prefix down to the stripped path. That last part is what bit you. The compose example ships `PUBLIC_GATEWAY_URL: http://localhost:8787/lobu` and sets no `AUTH_COOKIE_DOMAIN`. Behind a reverse proxy on your own domain, the browser origin no longer matches that configured origin, so the org link got built against the subdomain zone while the app was served from the apex — hence being able to register but then 404ing on models, chats, and everything else. Org scope is resolved from the Host header — `{org}.{zone}`, where the zone comes from `AUTH_COOKIE_DOMAIN` or falls back to the hostname in `PUBLIC_GATEWAY_URL`. So once you've created an org, the app sends you to a subdomain, and if your reverse proxy only forwards the apex you get a host with no resolvable org. Scope resolution then throws at the bare origin and the UI renders as 404s, which lines up with "no models, no chats, all sorts of 404 errors". Two things you can try right now, both without code changes: Point a wildcard at the container. If you can add `*.lobu-example.com` to DNS and your proxy, and set `PUBLIC_GATEWAY_URL=https://lobu-example.com` plus `AUTH_COOKIE_DOMAIN=.lobu-example.com`, the existing subdomain path should work as designed. This is the closest to how the hosted version runs, so it's the best-tested route. If wildcards aren't an option, note that path-based routing already partly exists — the frontend has an `/$owner/...` route, so `https://lobu-example.com/your-org/...` may get you further than the apex alone. I'd treat this as a workaround rather than a supported mode; there's no self-host flag today that makes it the default, and I haven't verified the whole app under it. On the actual ask — making path-based the supported setup for self-hosting — I think that's the right direction, since requiring wildcard DNS is a real barrier for anyone behind a single reverse proxy. I don't want to half-do it though: the pieces that need to agree are host-based scope extraction, the post-org-creation redirect, and auth cookie scoping (cookies on a shared path don't isolate orgs the way separate subdomains do, so that needs thought rather than a quick switch). Leaving this open as the tracking issue for that. Could you share what your proxy is (nginx/Caddy/Traefik) and whether wildcard DNS is available to you? That tells me whether the wildcard route unblocks you today, and it's useful input on how common the constraint is. --- COMMENT by bilogic --- Thanks, I'm using nginx proxy manager, likely moving to Caddy/Traefik. I do have wildcard certs in place today, but I would need a separate domain just for lobu, because today it is, https://service.my-domain.com, and I have many services on my homelab, it's going to be confusing to mix them up. =================== ISSUE #2184 =================== `latest` docker image should be tagged to release, not every push [CLOSED/COMPLETED] by bilogic LABELS: bug BODY: 1. The `latest` should tied to official releases, e.g. 14.2.0 instead of every other commit such as `20260724-034552` 2. It's quite impossible to figure out which is 14.2.0 --- COMMENT by buremba --- Both points are fair and this is a real packaging bug, not just a preference. You're right that `latest` currently moves on every push to `main`. The build workflow tags each image with a UTC timestamp and also pushes `latest` on the default branch, so `latest` tracks the tip of main rather than a release. For a self-hoster that means `docker pull ...:latest` gives you whatever merged most recently, which is not what the tag implies. On point 2, the reason you can't find a `14.2.0` image is that no such tag exists — the npm packages are versioned (14.2.0, 14.3.0) but the images are only ever tagged with the timestamp, so there's currently no way to map an image back to a release version at all. That's the more serious half of this report. One constraint worth flagging so the fix doesn't surprise you: our production deploy uses Flux, whose ImagePolicy matches the `^(\d{8})-(\d{6})$` timestamp pattern, and that policy lives in a separate repo. So the timestamp tags have to keep being published — the fix is to *add* semver tags (`14.3.0`, `14.3`, `14`) and repoint `latest` at the release build, not to change the existing scheme. That makes it an additive change to the release workflow. Marking this as a bug. Until it lands, pin the explicit timestamp tag you've tested rather than `latest`, since `latest` will keep moving under you. --- COMMENT by buremba --- Good catch, both parts were real. PR #2241 has the fix. `latest` was being pushed on every commit to main, which is why it kept landing on things like `20260724-034552`. It now only moves when a release is actually published, and the images get a semver tag at the same time, so `ghcr.io/lobu-ai/lobu-app:14.3.0` will work from the next release onward. Prereleases get their version tag but don't move `latest`. The timestamp tags aren't going away — our deploy automation selects images by that pattern, so they keep getting pushed on every main build. They just stop being what `latest` points at. One thing worth flagging: this takes effect from the next release, so `14.3.0` and earlier won't be retroactively tagged. Once it's out, pinning a version in your compose file is the safer setup anyway, and I've added a comment in `docker-compose.example.yml` showing that.

content.content: =================== ISSUE #2186 =================== `@lobu/cli@14.3.0` cannot be found [OPEN] by bilogic LABELS: bug BODY: **Describe the bug** ``` root@sqlserver2025:/# npx @lobu/cli@latest Need to install the following packages: @lobu/cli@14.3.0 Ok to proceed? (y) y npm ERR! code E404 npm ERR! 404 Not Found - GET https://registry.npmjs.org/@lobu%2fplugin-api - Not found npm ERR! 404 npm ERR! 404 '@lobu/plugin-api@14.3.0' is not in this registry. npm ERR! 404 npm ERR! 404 Note that you can also install from a npm ERR! 404 tarball, folder, http url, or git url. npm ERR! A complete log of this run can be found in: npm ERR! /root/.npm/_logs/2026-07-24T05_23_38_972Z-debug-0.log ``` **To Reproduce** Steps to reproduce the behavior: 1. Run `npx @lobu/cli@14.3.0 init` **Expected behavior** Command should run/install lobu **Screenshots** No **Environment** - Runtime (local/systemd/managed host): docker + local - Platform (Slack/Telegram/Discord/etc.): telegram - Lobu version: N/A **Additional context** No --- COMMENT by buremba --- Confirmed, and this is a release-blocking break on our side — thanks for the clear repro. What happened: `@lobu/cli@14.3.0` is on npm and is `latest`, but two packages it needs transitively were never created on the registry. `@lobu/plugin-api` and `@lobu/plugin-host` both have zero published versions, while `@lobu/worker@14.3.0` (a direct dep of the CLI) declares hard pins on `@lobu/plugin-api@14.3.0` and `@lobu/plugin-host@14.3.0`. So the install resolves the CLI fine and then 404s on the transitive dep, exactly as your log shows. Root cause is a first-publish bootstrap gap, not a bad version number. npm returns E404 on the *first* publish of a scoped package when the CI token is a granular access token, because the token's allow-list can't name a package that doesn't exist yet. Our publish script actually detects this and prints a bootstrap message, but it collects the blocked packages and only sets a non-zero exit at the very end — after the packages that depend on them have already been pushed. That's how a release went out with dependents published and their dependencies missing. Fix is in two parts: a one-time manual bootstrap publish of `@lobu/plugin-api` and `@lobu/plugin-host` by an org owner (then registering them as trusted publishers so CI takes over), and making the publish script fail *before* publishing any dependent of a blocked package rather than after. I'll do the bootstrap first so `npx @lobu/cli@latest` starts working without you needing a new version. No good workaround in the meantime, since the missing packages simply aren't on the registry — the Docker image is the working path until the bootstrap lands. I'll comment here when it's published. --- COMMENT by buremba --- Correction and expansion after digging into the published tarball — the problem is bigger than the two packages in the original report, and the `0.0.0` pins make it worse. `@lobu/worker@14.3.0` (a direct dep of the CLI) declares **six** `@lobu` plugin deps, none of which exist on the registry: ``` @lobu/plugin-api = 14.3.0 (0 versions published) @lobu/plugin-host = 14.3.0 (0 versions published) @lobu/plugin-conversations = 0.0.0 (0 versions published) @lobu/plugin-mcp = 0.0.0 (0 versions published) @lobu/plugin-media = 0.0.0 (0 versions published) @lobu/plugin-memory = 0.0.0 (0 versions published) @lobu/plugin-toolkit = 0.0.0 (0 versions published) ``` The installer reported `@lobu/plugin-api` first and stopped, which is why the original report only named one. The ones pinned at `0.0.0` are worse than the 404s: `0.0.0` is the placeholder version those packages carry in-repo because they're marked `private: true`, so that constraint can never be satisfied by any future release. Two distinct root causes, both in `scripts/publish-packages.mjs`: 1. `rewriteWorkspaceRefs()` rewrites `workspace:*` to whatever version it reads off disk, with no check that the target is published (or even publishable). For a `private: true` package it happily writes the placeholder `0.0.0` into the released manifest. It should hard-fail when a to-be-released package depends on something outside the release set. 2. The first-publish E404 handler collects blocked packages but only sets `exitCode = 1` after the loop, so dependents still go out even though their dependencies didn't. It should abort before releasing any dependent of a blocked package. These are not just manifest bugs. The released tarball's compiled output really does require those modules at runtime: ``` package/dist/runtime/plugin-composition.js:6: require("@lobu/plugin-host") package/dist/runtime/plugin-composition.js:7: require("@lobu/plugin-mcp") package/dist/runtime/plugin-composition.js:9: require("@lobu/plugin-memory") package/dist/runtime/transcript-snapshot.js:46: require("@lobu/plugin-toolkit") package/dist/embedded/mcp-cli-commands.js:10: require("@lobu/plugin-mcp") package/dist/gateway/gateway-integration.js:9: require("@lobu/plugin-toolkit") ``` `packages/agent-worker` builds with plain `tsc`, which transpiles but does not bundle, so those bare specifiers survive into `dist` and must resolve from `node_modules` at runtime. Even if the manifest were fixed to stop requesting them, the code would still crash on require. So there are two viable fixes, and the choice is a real architecture decision rather than a formality: - **Release them.** Flip the five `private: true` plugin packages to public, give them real versions, and register them as trusted publishers. Keeps the current runtime-resolution model; cost is five more public packages whose API surface we're then implicitly committing to. - **Bundle them.** Switch `packages/agent-worker`'s release build from bare `tsc` to a bundling step that inlines the plugin packages into `dist`, and drop the deps from the manifest entirely. Keeps them private and shrinks our public surface. This is what `packages/server` already does via `scripts/build-server-bundle.mjs`, so there's precedent in-repo. Bundling looks like the better fit — these plugins are internal composition units, not a public API, and their `0.0.0` versions suggest they were never intended to be consumed standalone. But it's the heavier change, and it needs a check that nothing else depends on them resolving as separate modules at runtime. Either way the guard in cause 1 should land regardless, since that's what let a broken manifest ship silently. --- COMMENT by buremba --- The fix for this is merged (#2235). Summarising what was actually wrong, since it turned out to be more than the two missing packages I mentioned earlier. `@lobu/worker` depended on workspace packages that were never published, so installing it could never resolve. The publish script rewrote `workspace:*` to whatever version was on disk without ever checking the target was publishable, which is how a `0.0.0` placeholder for a private package ended up as a real constraint on the registry. Two changes. The publish script now refuses to publish a package whose `@lobu` dependency it doesn't publish, so this fails loudly at release time instead of silently producing a broken tarball. And `@lobu/worker` now ships an esbuild bundle with the whole `@lobu` graph inlined — its published manifest declares zero `@lobu` dependencies, which also means the release no longer depends on `@lobu/plugin-api` and `@lobu/plugin-host` being published first. Verified by packing the tarball and installing it into an empty directory outside the workspace: install succeeds, `import '@lobu/worker'` runs, the `lobu-worker` binary runs, and consumer `tsc` passes under node10, node16 and bundler resolution. Also rehearsed the full fleet — packed all nine tarballs and installed `@lobu/cli` from them, which is what `npx @lobu/cli` resolves. Worth being straight about the remaining step: this is merged but **not yet published**, so `npx @lobu/cli@14.3.0` will still fail until the next release goes out. I'll follow up here once it's on the registry and I've re-run the clean-install check against the real thing rather than local tarballs. Thanks for the report — the packing check that caught the rest of this is now a CI gate, so this class of breakage can't ship again. =================== ISSUE #2206 =================== Split-origin dev: GitHub App install 401 (?org= won't fix it) + missing connector-detail UI tests [OPEN] by buremba LABELS: BODY: Follow-up from lobu#2204 / owletto#593, recording the `pi-review` blocker and the test gap so neither gets re-litigated. ## 1. GitHub App install 401s in split-origin dev — and `?org=` will NOT fix it **Scope: dev-only.** Prod and `make dev` are co-hosted, emit relative `/lobu/...` URLs, keep the session cookie, and work (verified live). This only affects the `LOBU_API_PROXY` mode introduced in owletto#593, where the SPA runs on a Vite host against a remote API. **Symptom:** clicking Install on a GitHub App connector in that mode returns 401 "Sign in to your organization before installing the GitHub App." **Cause:** `appInstallUrl` correctly navigates to the *gateway* origin (OAuth `redirect_uri`s are registered there, not on the Vite host). The dev proxy deliberately rewrites session cookies host-only for localhost, so the cross-origin navigation carries no cookie. `resolveInstallOrgId` then resolves `?org=` → session → single-tenant fallback, and returns null on a multi-tenant gateway. **Do not "fix" this by proxying `/lobu` same-origin.** That was the original workaround removed in owletto#593. It sends the browser to the Vite host, which does not own the registered `redirect_uri`, so the callback breaks. It would regress Slack, which currently works. **Threading `?org=` into the install URL does not work either.** `resolveRequestedOrgId` (`packages/server/src/gateway/routes/public/install-org.ts`) resolves the slug and then gates on `getCachedMembershipRole(orgId, userId)`, where `readUserId` reads only the session context. No cookie → no user → membership check cannot run → null. This is deliberate: "so a stray `?org=` can't select a foreign tenant." **The real constraint:** GitHub App install requires an authenticated session on the gateway; split-origin dev deliberately withholds the cookie from that origin. Any genuine fix has to authenticate against the remote gateway directly (e.g. PAT handoff / signing in on the gateway origin first), not pass a hint in the URL. Slack is unaffected — its `oauth-code-exchange` start route explicitly permits a logged-out start and funnels through the claim flow. ## 2. Missing UI regression tests `pi-review` flagged `tests_adequate: false`. Verification for these surfaces was live browser driving (real evidence, but not persistent regression protection). Unit tests currently cover the install-URL helpers only. =================== ISSUE #2231 ===================
Docker app image ships no lobu CLI — no CLI configuration path for self-hosters [OPEN] by buremba
LABELS: bug 
BODY:
Split out of #2151. Blocks Docker self-hosters from any CLI-based configuration.

`docker/app/Dockerfile`'s runtime stage copies `packages/core`, `plugin-api`, `plugin-host`, `plugin-toolkit`, `plugin-memory`, `plugin-conversations`, `plugin-media`, `plugin-mcp`, `agent-worker`, `connector-sdk`, `connectors`, `embeddings`, `connector-worker`, `server`, and `owletto` — but never `packages/cli`. `start.sh` execs the server bundle directly, so no `lobu` binary is ever installed or on PATH.

Consequence: a Docker self-hoster cannot run any `lobu ...` command. In #2151 a user was told to run `lobu providers create` to point at a local ollama and had no way to do it, then tried editing `/app/config/provision.json` (see below) as a workaround. Every CLI-documented workflow is unreachable on Docker; the web UI is the only configuration surface.

This is currently compounded by #2186 — `npx @lobu/cli@latest` also fails, because `@lobu/plugin-api` and `@lobu/plugin-host` were never published to npm. So right now there is no CLI path at all for a Docker user, from inside or outside the container.

Fix: ship the CLI in the app image so `docker exec <container> lobu providers ...` works. Worth confirming the size cost is acceptable, and that the CLI resolves its workspace deps against the hoisted `node_modules` layout the image already uses.

Separate small thing found while triaging: the user reported editing `/app/config/provision.json`. That filename appears nowhere in the repo and nothing reads it. If it's referenced in docs or in any CLI/server output, that reference should be removed — worth a grep outside this repo (docs site, templates) since it isn't in-tree.

--- COMMENT by buremba ---
Measured the size cost this calls for before picking an approach.

The CLI declares 68 dependencies. 41 of those are already in the app image because the server depends on them too, so the real delta is the 27 CLI-only ones:

`@clack/prompts, @inquirer/prompts, @opentelemetry/* (5), chalk, commander, dotenv, embedded-postgres, esbuild, isomorphic-git, jimp, jiti, ky, marked, marked-terminal, open, ora, playwright, playwright-vanilla, sharp, tar, vite, winston, yaml`

Most are small, but `embedded-postgres`, `playwright`, `playwright-vanilla`, `sharp`, `vite` and `esbuild` are not, and this image already installs a Chromium via patchright. Also worth noting the builder stage doesn't currently build the CLI at all — it's stubbed out at Dockerfile:51 purely so `bun install` resolves — so shipping it means adding a build step as well as the runtime COPY.

That makes it a genuine tradeoff rather than a one-line fix, so flagging the options instead of just picking:

1. Ship the whole CLI. Every documented `lobu ...` workflow works via `docker exec`. Costs the 27 deps above.
2. Bundle only the config/provisioning commands with esbuild, the way `server.bundle.mjs` is already built. Keeps the image lean and unblocks the #2151 ollama case, but then `lobu` inside the container is a subset of the real CLI, which is its own docs problem.
3. Rely on the npx path. #2186's fix has landed on a branch (#2235), so `npx @lobu/cli@latest` will work from the host once released — though that's outside the container, which doesn't help anyone whose only access is `docker exec`.

Leaning towards 1 for predictability, since a partial `lobu` that silently lacks commands is the kind of thing that costs more support time than image size does. Not implementing it yet pending a call on that.

On the separate finding: I re-grepped and `provision.json` still appears nowhere in this repo, so wherever the user got that filename it isn't in-tree — likely the docs site, which is tracked separately.

=================== ISSUE #2244 ===================
Spawned binaries can bypass the egress allowlist (allowNet: true) [OPEN] by buremba
LABELS: bug 
BODY:
## What

Spawned binaries registered by the embedded worker run with `allowNet: true` (`just-bash-bootstrap.ts`), which becomes `--share-net` under bwrap and `(allow network*)` under sandbox-exec. They therefore have unrestricted host networking.

The code's stated control is the proxy:

> Spawned binaries reach the network through HTTP_PROXY → gateway, which already enforces the per-agent domain allowlist.

That holds only for a binary that *chooses* to honor `HTTP_PROXY`. It is a convention, not an enforcement boundary. `curl --noproxy '*'`, or any tool that ignores the variable, connects directly and never touches the allowlist.

## Why it matters more now

This is **pre-existing** — `allowNet: true` and the `/nix/store` + `lobu` registration are on `main` today, so `curl`/`git` already run this way. But connector-contributed agent tooling (#2243) makes `gh` registrable, and `gh` is shell-capable: aliases and extensions run arbitrary commands. Combined with a leased `GH_TOKEN` in the environment, a bypass route becomes materially more interesting to an attacker than it was for `curl` alone.

## Bounded today

Under the shipped chart `containerSecurityContext` (drop ALL + RuntimeDefault seccomp), `probeSandboxStrategy` returns `none` and no spawned binary registers at all. Reaching this requires an operator to first enable bwrap (`SYS_ADMIN` or a Localhost seccomp profile permitting `unshare`) — documented in `charts/lobu/values.yaml`.

=================== ISSUE #2231 ===================
Docker app image ships no lobu CLI — no CLI configuration path for self-hosters [OPEN] by buremba
LABELS: bug 
BODY:
Split out of #2151. Blocks Docker self-hosters from any CLI-based configuration.

`docker/app/Dockerfile`'s runtime stage copies `packages/core`, `plugin-api`, `plugin-host`, `plugin-toolkit`, `plugin-memory`, `plugin-conversations`, `plugin-media`, `plugin-mcp`, `agent-worker`, `connector-sdk`, `connectors`, `embeddings`, `connector-worker`, `server`, and `owletto` — but never `packages/cli`. `start.sh` execs the server bundle directly, so no `lobu` binary is ever installed or on PATH.

Consequence: a Docker self-hoster cannot run any `lobu ...` command. In #2151 a user was told to run `lobu providers create` to point at a local ollama and had no way to do it, then tried editing `/app/config/provision.json` (see below) as a workaround. Every CLI-documented workflow is unreachable on Docker; the web UI is the only configuration surface.

This is currently compounded by #2186 — `npx @lobu/cli@latest` also fails, because `@lobu/plugin-api` and `@lobu/plugin-host` were never published to npm. So right now there is no CLI path at all for a Docker user, from inside or outside the container.

Fix: ship the CLI in the app image so `docker exec <container> lobu providers ...` works. Worth confirming the size cost is acceptable, and that the CLI resolves its workspace deps against the hoisted `node_modules` layout the image already uses.

Separate small thing found while triaging: the user reported editing `/app/config/provision.json`. That filename appears nowhere in the repo and nothing reads it. If it's referenced in docs or in any CLI/server output, that reference should be removed — worth a grep outside this repo (docs site, templates) since it isn't in-tree.

--- COMMENT by buremba ---
Measured the size cost this calls for before picking an approach.

The CLI declares 68 dependencies. 41 of those are already in the app image because the server depends on them too, so the real delta is the 27 CLI-only ones:

`@clack/prompts, @inquirer/prompts, @opentelemetry/* (5), chalk, commander, dotenv, embedded-postgres, esbuild, isomorphic-git, jimp, jiti, ky, marked, marked-terminal, open, ora, playwright, playwright-vanilla, sharp, tar, vite, winston, yaml`

Most are small, but `embedded-postgres`, `playwright`, `playwright-vanilla`, `sharp`, `vite` and `esbuild` are not, and this image already installs a Chromium via patchright. Also worth noting the builder stage doesn't currently build the CLI at all — it's stubbed out at Dockerfile:51 purely so `bun install` resolves — so shipping it means adding a build step as well as the runtime COPY.

That makes it a genuine tradeoff rather than a one-line fix, so flagging the options instead of just picking:

1. Ship the whole CLI. Every documented `lobu ...` workflow works via `docker exec`. Costs the 27 deps above.
2. Bundle only the config/provisioning commands with esbuild, the way `server.bundle.mjs` is already built. Keeps the image lean and unblocks the #2151 ollama case, but then `lobu` inside the container is a subset of the real CLI, which is its own docs problem.
3. Rely on the npx path. #2186's fix has landed on a branch (#2235), so `npx @lobu/cli@latest` will work from the host once released — though that's outside the container, which doesn't help anyone whose only access is `docker exec`.

Leaning towards 1 for predictability, since a partial `lobu` that silently lacks commands is the kind of thing that costs more support time than image size does. Not implementing it yet pending a call on that.

On the separate finding: I re-grepped and `provision.json` still appears nowhere in this repo, so wherever the user got that filename it isn't in-tree — likely the docs site, which is tracked separately.

11	`latest` was published on **every** default-branch push, so self-hosters pulling `ghcr.io/lobu-ai/lobu-app:latest` got an arbitrary commit, and no tag identified a release at all — you could not pull `14.2.0` (issue #2184, external user `bilogic`). 13	**The trap that would have made the whole fix a no-op:** releases created with `GITHUB_TOKEN` **do not trigger release-event workflows**. `release-please.yml` had `token: ${{ secrets.RELEASE_PLEASE_TOKEN || secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}`, so under the fallback the new `release:` trigger would never fire and everything would look correct while doing nothing. The fallback is now removed and the workflow fails loudly if the token is absent (it IS configured on the repo). `helm-chart.yml` and `mac-release.yml` consume release events too and get the same protection. This was caught by `make review-fix`, not by me.
14

Prod's HelmRelease pins an explicit timestamp carrying the `# {"$imagepolicy": ...}` marker that ImageUpdateAutomation rewrites, so **nothing in the deploy path ever resolves `latest`**. The chart's `values.yaml` default `tag: "latest"` is overridden by that marker and only affects ad-hoc chart installs.
